messages.subject: Difference between RMSEA and SRMR
parts: I try to learn more about RMSEA and SRMR. I know that if the sample size of my study increases, RMSEA will decrease (David Kenny, 2015). How about SRMR?  From Kenny's website, he said that SRMR is a positively biased measure and that bias is greater for small N and for low df studies because the SRMR is an absolute measure of fit, a value of zero indicates perfect fit. Does it mean small N or low df will have low value of SRMR as a result? What if I have a good result of SRMR(e.g. <0.06) and a poor result of RMSEA(e.g. >0.08)?  Should I collect more data for it? Thank you so much.

messages.author: b430763ad49e6cd0
messages.subject: Re: Difference between RMSEA and SRMR
parts:
Hey, 

Disclaimer: I am no expert in SEM / CFA. I am still learning a lot myself, so read this with a critical mindset. 

First, by positively biased he means that the SRMR tends to be larger than it should be, and that this upward bias is more pronounced for small sample sizes (N) and low df.
. Does it mean small N or low df will have low value of SRMR as a result?

So, no. Also, by saying it like you do, you seem to imply that the SRMR would always be too large (i.e. positive bias) when having a small N and/or low df. This is not true. However, it can be that your model is correctly specified, while your SRMR is large. This can happen as you say Kenny says on his website: (partly) because of having a small N and/or low df. I believe this is because of sampling error is more pronounced in small samples, which affects the residual covariances. As the latter is used to compute the SRMR, this would induce positive bias in the SRMR.
What if I have a good result of SRMR(e.g. <0.06) and a poor result of RMSEA(e.g. >0.08)?  Should I collect more data for it? Thank you so much.

This probably depends on a lot of things that other people are more suited to answer for you. However, today I read a paper (Kenny, D. A., Kaniskan, B., & McCoach, D. B. (2015)), where they discourage people to use the RMSEA in small samples with low df. This might be an interesting read for you (see below for the link). 

Whether you should collect more data or not, I don't know. To answer this, it might be useful to also tell us what your sample size is ;) 

http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0049124114543236

Btw: questions like these could instead be asked on SEMNET. There are many experts there who are actively helping each other out, and luckily for us; beginners also :) 

Good luck,
Amonet
